strengths: The paper presents a clear and practically useful inference-time framework for controlling an unconditional 3D anatomical diffusion model without retraining it for each constraint.
Representing size, position, and coarse shape through differentiable zeroth-, first-, and second-order moments is simple, interpretable, and naturally supports component-wise composition.

The experimental section is broad: it includes multiple conditional-model baselines, guidance-strength sweeps, loss ablations, multi-component experiments, qualitative visualizations, and a biomechanical simulation example.

The reported results provide credible evidence that moment guidance improves target fidelity while generally retaining sample quality, and the ablation in Table 1 supports partial independent control of the three attribute classes.
The method and training setup are described reasonably well, including architectures, loss weights, sampling configurations, preprocessing, and simulation parameters.
weaknesses: The main technical idea is incremental: applying differentiable moment losses through established diffusion posterior or universal guidance is straightforward, and the paper provides limited new theoretical or algorithmic insight beyond this application and loss design.

The evaluation is partly circular. Morphological quality and conditional fidelity are largely computed from the same masses, centroids, and covariance-derived features optimized by the guidance loss. Independent evidence such as expert assessment, topology metrics, surface-quality measures, or downstream performance over a substantial cohort is missing.

The compositional comparison is not convincing. The implicit baseline independently drops each of six conditions with probability 0.1, making zero- or one-component training configurations extremely rare. Its severe degradation for few conditions is therefore an expected training-distribution failure and does not substantiate the broad claim that conditional approaches require retraining. At six components, it is comparable to or better than the proposed method on several metrics.

Experiments use only 596 automatically segmented and manually filtered cases, with evaluation on the validation split rather than a separately held-out test set. The paper reports no confidence intervals, repeated seeds, significance tests, cross-dataset validation, or robustness to out-of-distribution and pathological targets.

Second-order moments constrain only an ellipsoidal summary. They cannot specify local anatomy, topology, branching, curvature, or fine-scale simulation-critical features. The qualitative examples involving branched structures do not demonstrate control over those complex properties; they merely match their global moments.

The biomechanics demonstration consists of one toy patient with three manually defined RV sizes. It does not validate simulation readiness broadly and cannot support the conclusion that the method elucidates causal form-function relationships.

Anatomical validity remains insufficiently assessed. The authors acknowledge disconnected or duplicated structures, but provide neither failure rates nor topology-aware comparisons, and there is no clinical-expert evaluation of realism.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code or trained-model release is stated, target-selection and manual quality-control protocols are underspecified, computational cost is absent, and the finite-element solver is in-house. Potential clinical misuse and limitations of synthetic anatomy are also not discussed.

strengths: The manuscript is clearly motivated and presents an intuitive inference-time mechanism for controlling 3D anatomical generation without retraining the underlying unconditional diffusion model. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/235435b23e0346d7a88501fb8a46948b/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
Representing size, position, and shape using zeroth-, first-, and normalized second-order moments is simple, differentiable, interpretable, and naturally supports component-wise composition.
The paper is generally well organized and includes several useful comparisons, ablations over individual loss terms, morphological and point-cloud metrics, and clear qualitative visualizations.
The inpainting and finite-element example illustrates a potentially valuable connection between controllable anatomical generation and downstream biophysical simulation.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited. The central technique is established gradient-based diffusion guidance applied to straightforward moment-matching losses; the paper does not provide a substantial new algorithmic or theoretical insight beyond this application and decomposition.

The evidence for anatomical realism is inadequate. Many evaluation features are the same moments explicitly optimized by the guidance loss, making improvements in morphological space partly circular. Point-cloud distances also do not establish anatomical or topological validity, and there is no expert assessment, validity rate, overlap/connectivity analysis, or task-based validation. The paper itself acknowledges disconnected vessels and duplicated structures but does not quantify their frequency.

The compositional comparison is not convincing. The implicit baseline uses per-component dropout probability 0.1, so its fully unconditional configuration occurs with probability approximately 10^-6 for six components. Its catastrophic zero-component result is therefore expected and does not demonstrate that conditional models inherently require retraining. Alternative dropout schedules or baselines designed for arbitrary subsets are needed. At six components, the implicit baseline is competitive with or better than the proposed method on several metrics.

Experiments use only 596 automatically segmented, manually filtered cases from one dataset, with an unspecified filtering protocol. There is no external-dataset evaluation, pathological-cohort analysis, or evidence that the method generalizes beyond this cardiac label set.

Reported results use only 100–200 generated samples and provide no confidence intervals, statistical tests, multiple training seeds, or variability analysis. Consequently, several modest metric differences cannot be judged reliable.

The claim of disentanglement is supported only by aggregate moment errors. It is not assessed whether controlling one moment changes unreported anatomy, inter-label relationships, local geometry, or clinically important features not captured by ellipsoidal summaries.

The biomechanical study is only a three-case toy demonstration using one patient, hand-selected twofold/half-volume edits, simplified material assumptions, and no uncertainty or validation. It cannot support the conclusion that the framework elucidates causal structure-function relationships or produces generally simulation-ready anatomy.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code or trained models are identified, and important details such as the magnitude of denominator stabilization noise, exact sampler and update implementation, target-selection protocol, random seeds, training variability, and computational cost of decoding and backpropagating at every denoising step are missing.

Overall, the paper has a useful engineering idea and polished presentation, but the limited novelty, potentially unfair key baseline, circular aspects of the evaluation, and lack of rigorous anatomical validation leave the main realism and compositionality claims insufficiently supported for a top-tier AI venue.

strengths: Clear, useful contribution: an unconditional 3D diffusion model can be controlled at inference time using differentiable geometric moments, avoiding retraining for each constraint.
The formulation is simple and interpretable, with separate losses for size, position, and scale-normalized shape that can be applied label-wise and combined flexibly.

The disentanglement experiments provide concrete positive evidence: activating an individual loss substantially improves its corresponding fidelity while largely preserving unconstrained attributes, and the combined loss performs well across all three attributes.

The evaluation includes several conditional-generation baselines, multiple morphological and point-cloud metrics, qualitative visualizations, and ablations over guidance strength and constrained components.
The cardiovascular application is relevant and technically challenging, and the inpainting-plus-biomechanical-simulation example illustrates a plausible downstream use.
The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, with helpful diagrams and substantial implementation detail in the appendix.
weaknesses: The strongest compositional-baseline result is not fully convincing. The implicit model drops each of six components with probability 0.1 during training, making examples with zero or one active component extraordinarily rare; its collapse for those test conditions is therefore expected from the training distribution. A baseline trained by uniformly sampling subset sizes or constraint masks is needed before concluding that conditional models must be retrained for varying component counts.

The experiments report only 100–200 generated samples per setting, without confidence intervals, significance tests, repeated training runs, or sensitivity to random seeds. This makes several relatively small metric differences difficult to interpret.

Moment matching constrains only coarse ellipsoidal properties. It cannot ensure local morphology, connectivity, topology, vessel branching, or other clinically important features. The paper acknowledges topological failures but does not quantify their frequency or include anatomical-expert assessment, weakening claims of realism and simulation readiness.

The biomechanical demonstration uses a single patient and a simplified, partly constructed ventricular geometry. It is a useful proof of concept but does not substantiate the broader claim that the framework elucidates causal structure–function relationships.
The approach requires decoding and backpropagating through the full 3D volume at every denoising step, yet runtime, memory consumption, and overhead relative to conditional sampling are not reported.

Generality is demonstrated only on one curated cardiac dataset generated partly from automated segmentations. The manual exclusion criteria, number of reviewers, and reproducibility of the filtering procedure are unspecified, and there is no evaluation on another organ, dataset, resolution, or out-of-distribution constraint range.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: guidance-weight tuning is described only qualitatively, some training and optimization details are missing, and no code or pretrained-model availability statement is provided.

The underlying technical idea—using low-order moment losses for gradient-guided diffusion—is elegant but fairly incremental; the paper's competitiveness rests on the application and empirical evidence rather than a major methodological advance.

strengths: CardioComposer offers a useful and interpretable inference-time mechanism for controlling the size, position, shape, and orientation of individual structures in 3D anatomical diffusion models without retraining the generative model.

The moment-based objectives are simple, differentiable, and composable. The paper clearly explains how zeroth-, first-, and normalized second-order moments support both attribute-specific and multi-structure control.

The experimental study is relatively broad: it includes several conditional-model baselines, guidance-weight sweeps, disentanglement and composition experiments, a toy ellipsoid study, dataset-scaling and editing-range analyses, topology measurements, and a biomechanical case study.
Evaluation combines conditional-fidelity, morphological-distribution, point-cloud, and topology metrics rather than relying solely on qualitative examples.

The appendix provides useful architectural, preprocessing, guidance-weight, and simulation details, and the paper candidly reports failure under extreme edits and increased topological errors under guidance.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is moderate: the method largely applies established loss-based diffusion guidance to standard low-order geometric moments. The paper does not provide a deeper theoretical or algorithmic advance explaining when compositional guidance should remain stable or preserve the anatomical prior.

The strongest practical claim—producing realistic or simulation-ready anatomy—is undermined by the topology results. Guidance increases connected-component errors for several important structures, including the aorta, pulmonary artery, and inferior vena cava, yet no topology-preserving mechanism, failure rate at the selected operating point, or robust rejection strategy is evaluated.

The compositional comparison is not fully convincing. The principal baseline uses independent condition dropout, making low-condition and unconditional configurations extremely rare by construction; its poor performance for few constraints is therefore partly an artifact of the training scheme. Stronger test-time energy-guidance alternatives, better-balanced conditional training, and all conditional architectures are not compared in this experiment.

Some realism metrics are built from the same low-order moments that the proposed method directly optimizes, making that portion of the evaluation partly circular. Point-cloud metrics help, but there is no blinded expert assessment, surface-quality analysis, or task-based validation over a substantial cohort.

Generality beyond the cardiac dataset is supported almost entirely by qualitative examples. The aorta, spine, and knee experiments lack quantitative fidelity, realism, topology, and baseline comparisons.

The biomechanical evidence consists of one illustrative case and does not establish the claimed causal or broadly useful form-function relationship. It lacks replication, sensitivity analysis, and validation that the edited samples remain physiologically credible.

Results generally omit uncertainty intervals, repeated-run variability, and statistical testing. Baseline hyperparameter selection and compute matching are also insufficiently documented, making it difficult to determine whether comparisons are robust and fair.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: important details such as optimizer and scheduling choices, random seeds, exact numerical stabilization used in moment denominators, hardware/training cost, and code availability are absent. Eigenvector-based orientation guidance also needs discussion of instability near repeated eigenvalues.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem: interpretable, inference-time control of 3D multi-label anatomical generators without retraining for every new constraint.
The moment-based losses are simple, differentiable, and easy to compose across anatomical labels. The presentation of mass, centroid, and covariance control is generally clear.

The experimental scope is broader than a single proof of concept, including cardiac generation, attribute ablations, multi-part control, out-of-distribution target scaling, topology analysis, and qualitative demonstrations on aorta, spine, and knee data.
The appendix reports useful implementation details and openly reveals important failure modes, including increasing connected-component errors under guidance and severe degradation for extreme edits.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited. The method is essentially standard loss-based diffusion guidance applied to classical zeroth-, first-, and second-order geometric moments; the paper does not provide a substantial algorithmic or theoretical advance beyond this combination.

The strongest baseline comparison is not convincing. For compositional control, the implicit conditional baseline independently drops six conditions with probability 0.1, making the fully unconditional configuration occur with probability approximately 10^-6. The paper acknowledges that this causes the baseline's catastrophic zero- and one-constraint results, so Table 1 largely demonstrates a deliberately imbalanced training scheme rather than an inherent advantage of the proposed method. Balanced subset sampling and stronger inference-time guidance baselines are missing.

Several evaluations are partly circular: the morphological realism metrics are constructed from the same masses, centroids, and covariance-derived features that the proposed losses directly optimize. Improved scores in that feature space therefore provide weak evidence of anatomical realism. Point-cloud metrics help, but there is no expert assessment, surface-quality analysis, or sufficiently comprehensive topology evaluation.

The paper overstates control of complex non-convex anatomy. First and second moments specify only a coarse equivalent ellipsoid, and many anatomically distinct, disconnected, or pathological shapes share those moments. The qualitative examples do not establish meaningful control over branching, local caliber, cross-sections, connectivity, or other clinically important geometry.

The appendix exposes a serious practical weakness: guided samples have more topological defects than unconditional samples, including roughly one extra component on average for the pulmonary artery and even higher error for the aorta. This conflicts with claims of realistic or simulation-ready anatomy, and filtering invalid samples is not an adequate resolution without reporting rejection rates and resulting bias.

The biomechanical study contains only one edited patient and three simulations. It changes geometry, meshing, and an artificially constructed RV wall simultaneously, provides no repeated trials or validation, and cannot support the claimed causal conclusions about anatomical form and function.

The claimed generality beyond cardiac anatomy is supported only by selected qualitative examples from separately trained models. There are no quantitative fidelity, realism, topology, or failure-rate results for the aorta, spine, and knee datasets.

Results lack uncertainty estimates, repeated-seed analysis, and statistical testing despite relatively small evaluation sets of 24 to 200 samples. Hyperparameters are experimentally tuned on the same data distribution used for evaluation, but the selection protocol and sensitivity are insufficiently documented.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code or trained models are identified, manual dataset filtering criteria are unspecified, and important training details such as random seeds, compute cost, exact preprocessing bounds, and complete architecture specifications are missing.

The paper does not adequately discuss risks associated with using anatomically invalid synthetic structures in medical-device evaluation or simulation studies. Given the documented topology failures, stronger safeguards and clearer limits on clinical interpretation are needed.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and practically useful inference-time framework for controlling unconditional 3D anatomical diffusion models without retraining; the ability to compose constraints across arbitrary labeled substructures is especially appealing.

The moment-based formulation is simple, interpretable, and differentiable, with sensible separation of size, position, and scale-normalized shape. The exposition and visual overview are generally clear.

The cardiac experiments cover conditional fidelity, realism, disentanglement, compositionality, editing range, topology, and dataset scaling, using both morphology- and point-cloud-based metrics. Comparisons against three conditioning architectures are more substantial than a purely qualitative demonstration.

The experiments provide convincing evidence that the method can control individual attributes while largely preserving unconstrained variation. The extension to multi-label unions, curved or branching structures, and several anatomical systems suggests broad applicability.

The biomechanical example usefully connects generative control to a downstream scientific workflow, while the appendix contains helpful architecture, training, guidance-weight, reconstruction, and out-of-distribution editing details. weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty is moderate: it combines standard geometric moments with established loss-based diffusion guidance. The paper should distinguish its technical contribution more sharply from prior energy-guided composition and ellipsoid-based control, particularly ProtComposer.

The central multi-part comparison is not fully convincing. Table 1 reports realism but not aggregate constraint fidelity, compares only against the implicit-conditioning baseline, and uses a dropout setup that the authors themselves explain makes partially conditioned and unconditional configurations poorly represented. Stronger subset-conditioning baselines or separately trained conditional models would make the comparison fairer.

Generality beyond cardiac anatomy is supported only by a few qualitative samples. Quantitative fidelity, realism, and topology results for the aorta, spine, and knee datasets are needed to substantiate the broad cross-anatomy claim.

Topological validity remains a significant concern for the intended simulation use case. Table 8 shows that guidance increases connected-component errors for several structures, sometimes substantially, yet the main evaluation does not report failure rates or demonstrate an effective filtering or topology-preserving strategy.

The biomechanical study contains only one edited anatomy and a simplified constructed RV wall. It is a useful proof of concept, but it does not support the stronger language about elucidating causal form-function relationships or establish physiological validity.

Reproducibility is incomplete: code or model availability is not stated, manual segmentation-quality filtering criteria are unspecified, the denominator-stabilizing noise magnitude is omitted, and results lack uncertainty estimates or sensitivity across training runs and random seeds.
